words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Bjarni mokaði vikri af túninu. Þar var gras áður; grasið var fóður kindanna. Siggi skoðaði túnið. Þar var lambið hans áður.
Ásta kastaði steini af túninu. Hún var hjá Sigga, og hann hreinsaði skóna. Á túninu var enn vikur.
words_with_history.note_en: Tún originally meant an enclosure or enclosed piece of land. English town shares its Germanic root; the meanings developed differently. On this farm, tún is the home field, not a town.

grammar.title: Nú og áður
grammar.rule: Nú kallar Siggi. Áður kallaði hann. Þegar askan féll, var dimmt.
grammar.note_en:
Past tense places a situation before the moment of speaking. The story now uses past narration. Direct speech can still use the present: Nú er matur means “Now there is food”. Einu sinni var dimmt means “Once it was dark”; í gær means “yesterday”, áður “earlier”, and þá “then”. These expressions locate the situation, but do not themselves create a past form.

Vera, “to be”, is irregular. The third person means talking about someone or something: he, she or it, or a name. Var is “was” with a singular third-person subject, while voru is “were” with a plural subject: Himinninn var rauður, “The sky was red”; kýrnar voru í fjósinu, “The cows were in the cowshed”. Það var dimmt means “It was dark”. Had is hafði: Hún hafði mig hjá Helgu means “She kept me beside Helga”. Here hafði expresses having; it is not an instruction to build a perfect tense.

A weak verb forms its past with a dental ending rather than by changing its main vowel alone. This chapter introduces only the -aði class. Replace final -a of the dictionary form with -aði for a singular third-person subject: moka → mokaði, “shovel → shovelled”; kalla → kallaði, “call → called”; hreinsa → hreinsaði, “clear → cleared”; kasta → kastaði, “throw → threw”. Bjarni mokaði vikri af túninu means “Bjarni shovelled pumice off the home field”. Helga hreinsaði skó means “Helga cleaned shoes”. Kasta takes a dative object: Óli kastaði vikri means “Óli threw pumice”. Learn the verb’s class with the word: this ending does not apply to every Icelandic verb.

Þegar means “when”. Þegar hann sagði ragnarök, var Ásta ekki glöð means “When he said Ragnarök, Ásta was not happy”. Learn the supplied when-clause as a whole pattern here. 

A few further past forms are supplied for reading as complete items: sagði “said”, spurði “asked”, fór/fóru “went”, kom “came”, sá “saw”, féll/féllu “fell”. The singular/plural pairs are not an invitation to construct other strong past forms. They remain supported reading items here and are never required gap answers. Baulaðu nú, Búkolla mín means “Moo now, my Búkolla!” It is one supplied story formula; commands are taught later. Allir, “everyone”, is likewise reading support, not a productive paradigm in this chapter.

Var also goes with ég: Ég var hér líka means “I was here too”; Í gær var ég inni means “Yesterday I was indoors”. These are the same past form with a first-person subject, the speaker. Hafa changes with number: with third-person subjects, hafði is singular and höfðu plural. Þær höfðu hey means “They had hay”. The table’s present and past contrasts have their own prose examples: Mamma kallar ekki nú (“Mother is not calling now”), mamma kallaði á mig (“Mother called me”), Nú hefur lambið hey (“Now the lamb has hay”), and Hún hafði mig hjá Helgu (“She kept me beside Helga”).

pronunciation_note.rule: In kallaði and mokaði, ð is a voiced dental fricative, like th in English this. The past ending is -aði; do not pronounce it as a separate English word. Contrast kallar with kallaði.
